The Washington Post reported on November 2nd that SpaceX has been in talks to buy Boost from EchoStar (NASDAQ: SATS) or partner with it. Nothing has been signed, and the structure is still open. The appeal is speed and cost. TD Cowen analyst Gregory Williams estimates a national network from scratch would cost upwards of $80 billion and take years. Verizon's CEO put the build at four to six years and $300 billion to $500 billion. Musk says two to three years. Boost brings customers, a brand and spectrum, and SpaceX already agreed to buy some EchoStar spectrum licenses for about $17 billion. T-Mobile's CEO sees no room for a SpaceX MVNO, though he is open to a resale deal for a complementary satellite product. AT&T closed its EchoStar spectrum deal in the third quarter. Verizon added 406,000 postpaid phone net additions, AT&T added 379,000, and T-Mobile raised full-year guidance. The catch is that Boost leases network access from AT&T and T-Mobile, and a change of control could let both end those agreements. Watch whether that risk derails any deal.

items.headline: Parents Are Missing the $1,000 Trump Account Deposit Because of One Form
items.summary: If you had a baby in 2025 or 2026, the federal government has $1,000 waiting for your child in a new Trump account. But automatically enrolled does not mean automatically paid. Jake FitzGerald of 24/7 Wall St. walks through the two separate steps families keep merging into one. First, claim the account at trumpaccounts.gov or in the app, since the Treasury has been opening accounts on its own since October. Second, file IRS Form 4547 to request the $1,000 federal seed. No form means no deposit. He also covers the fine print. Anyone can contribute up to $5,000 a year combined, and the $1,000 seed sits outside that cap. Employers can add up to $2,500, and Goldman Sachs, BlackRock and Nasdaq have said they will match the federal seed. The money goes into a U.S. stock index fund and stays locked until 18, after which it works like a traditional IRA. For tuition, a 529 plan is still likely the better tool.

items.headline: Adobe Exec Talks Strategy Behind New Partnership + ‘Global Sports Phenomenon’
items.summary: How is artificial intelligence changing the fan experience, and what does the future of sports engagement look like? In this NYSE Live interview, Marissa Dacay, Global Vice President of Enterprise Marketing at Adobe, discusses the company's partnership with BWT Alpine Formula One Team and how artificial intelligence is helping transform sports marketing and fan engagement. Kristen Scholer spoke with Dacay about AI-powered content creation, fan personalization, sports partnerships, digital experiences, generative AI, and evolving consumer behavior. A significant portion of the discussion focuses on Adobe's strategy within the sports industry. Through partnerships with leading teams, leagues, and global brands, the company helps organizations create more meaningful and personalized relationships with fans. The interview also explores Adobe's new role as the official AI fan experience partner of BWT Alpine Formula One Team. The collaboration leverages Adobe's technology platform to enhance content creation, audience engagement, and data-driven fan experiences. Another major theme is personalization at scale. Sports organizations increasingly depend on data and AI tools to better understand fan interests and deliver tailored experiences across multiple channels. The conversation further examines how AI is transforming content workflows. Adobe's technologies help organizations produce customized content more efficiently while supporting greater audience engagement and operational agility. The interview also highlights changes in digital discovery. As consumers increasingly interact with brands through AI-powered search platforms and large language model experiences, businesses must adapt their strategies to remain visible and relevant. Another key topic is fan participation. Today's audiences often want to do more than watch events unfold. They want to create, share, contribute, and become active participants in the communities surrounding their favorite teams and athletes. The discussion also explores Adobe Express and its role in enabling user-generated content creation. These tools allow fans to design customized graphics, social media posts, and other digital content connected to teams, players, and events. Additionally, Dacay discusses how generative AI is helping organizations foster stronger fan relationships by empowering users to actively tell their own stories and share their experiences across digital platforms. The conversation further highlights the global appeal of Formula One and the opportunities for technology-driven fan engagement within one of the world's fastest-growing sports properties. Another focus is the intersection of sports, technology, and business growth. Adobe believes enhanced digital experiences can drive stronger engagement, increase loyalty, and create new opportunities for brands and organizations. Looking ahead, Dacay expects artificial intelligence, personalization, content innovation, and fan participation to remain central themes shaping the future of sports and entertainment experiences. Throughout the discussion, Dacay shares perspectives on artificial intelligence, Formula One, sports marketing, customer experience, fan engagement, content creation, digital transformation, personalization, generative AI, and business growth.
